en: “The only child obtained at death’s door
Will be left sick,” she said.
“God will take our lives in this way,” she said.
Your dear mother Chyyyrdy
Grieved on her side.
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey
Bound and fastened once again,
Into the fold of her overskirt,
The child from the cradle,
Securing him firmly there.
Your capable mother Kanykey,
Revealing her widow’s plight,
Took powerless Chyyyrdy,
Her mother who had grown old,
Upon her moonlike back.
Walking straight ahead, her soul burned;
Unable to stand still, thirsty, her blood burned.
Unable to cross the ridge on foot,
Unable to reach a known place,
Unable to sleep on peaceful ground,
Your mother Kanykey
Could find no place upon the earth.
For two days in that isolated place
She went without lying down.
Two people upon one person
Went without room enough.
Her soles pounded against stone,
She grew thin as she went.
Wandering, weeping, walking on foot,
Your mother Kanykey went in misery.
Toward Temir Khan’s city
Your mother wandered, fleeing on foot;
Toward Karakan’s city
She walked on foot in grief.
Her joints weakened and wavered.
Her streaming tears
Glistened at her collarbone.
Her rib bones came apart;
The moonlike back that carried Chyyyrdy
Had flesh torn away in cupfuls.
With all her flanks rubbed raw,
Your sister-in-law, shrunk to a span,
Wounded every heart.
At every stride, without respite,
The flesh of her soles crumbled;
At each step it squelched,
The warrior’s blood trickling.
Yet if the fierce woman would not walk,
Her flylike soul cried out.
“The dear bird, a wild duck,
Flies over the plain without turning back,” she said.
Having seen so much, Kanykey
Went lamenting and weeping,
“For the child born from my womb,” she said.
“The wretched bird called the kite
Swoops in flight over the plain,” she said.
Your wretched mother Kanykey
Was wasting away as she went,
“For the child born from my belly,” she said.
“My ocean, my lord, would that you had not died!
Would that this poor soul had not known wandering!
Humiliation such as this,
O God, if you create living souls,
Never again grant it to your servant!
Alas, my forehead bone was crooked:
After my king passed away,
The days I was to see were meager!
The hair at my nape was wool:
When the sultan passed away,
My lot was to see days of calamity.
The Gray Belt left by the magnanimous one
I fasten at my waist as his gift.
To the city of my father Karakan,
O God, how shall I go wandering?!
My dear, long thick hair,
How shall I braid it down over my hips?
My lord Manas, would that you had not died!
To my father, the ruling khan’s city,
As though visiting my birth family,
Staggering in mourning,
How shall I look upon his face this year?!
To great Bukhara, the ruined city,
O God, shall I reach a corner and settle?
Fierce Ubaker, may you fare ill!
Bereft of my great one,
I, unfortunate and tormented,
Shall I earn the name of wanderer?
Revealing my widow’s plight,
To my father Karakan’s city,
With my aged mother Chyyyrdy
Riding upon my moonlike back,
How shall I make my way?
Alas, the deep pit dug for me!
O God, alas, my boiling misery!
Joined to them when tiny as a louse,
Parted from that wise household,
Have I scattered my gold like stones?
Carrying Semetey on my back,
Have I fled toward my birth family?”
Then your mother Kanykey,
If she would walk, lost her strength;
If Kanykey would not walk,
Her strength left her with crying and screaming.
Slashed like saddle straps,
Black blood ran from her calves.
The flesh of her heels rubbed raw,
Her life hurt without ceasing.
Worn out, her soul exhausted,
Her vatlike body wasted away.
The road to Bukhara was far;
She wept in torrents, unable to reach it.
Your mother, your swift steed, was humiliated.
Your poor mother Kanykey,
Revealing her widow’s plight,
Upon her moonlike back, the poor woman
Set the one who had borne Manas,
Chyyyrdy, to ride:
“At last I shall die one day.
Such is the command God has imposed;
Such is what I am destined to see!
Parted from this Kyrgyz people,
How can I refrain from lamenting?
Is this God’s command?
In place of my swift steed, my lord,
When I flee to Bukhara,
I shall make this mother my Mecca.
One glance at her fills my belly.
I have parted from my dear people;
I have no Mecca but my mother.
My river, the broad expanse of the lake,
My mother with the golden womb,
My elder who gave birth to the warrior!
Such is this shitty world;
I have no companion but my mother.
Pressed to my forehead, she is my shelter;
My queenly mother is my support!”
Wandering toward Bukhara, fleeing on foot,
Without a mount, fleeing on foot,
Her pacing gait quickened.
Your mother stepped lightly, ambling along.
The ridges in succession
She truly crossed now.
Through the barren desert thick with flies,
Without sparing her flylike soul,
Your mother truly strode onward now.
As though enemies came behind her,
Startled and hurrying without a halt,
For two days in a single hollow
She would not lie, but kept going.
Semetey, still a nursing infant,
Beneath your sister-in-law’s arm
Would not fit as she went.
Her threadlike life upon the plain
She disregarded as she went.
Though much tormented, her poor soul
Went onward without dying.
The flesh lost from her feet
She did not spare as she went.
This life passing, these days gone,
She did not see as she went.
This soul, more wretched than wretched,
Went onward without dying.
When she reached the broad bare ground,
Her worn boots flapped.
Your sister-in-law gave thanks to God.
Though she had seen so much hell,
She went on brightly.
The wind could not catch her trot.
With her thoughts given to ardor,
She trotted and ran along.
Left behind by her khan,
Kanykey took as her support
Her sole child, Semetey.
Running tirelessly, fleeing on foot,
Walking without weariness,
She fled with courage.
Dividing the hair on her crown in ten,
Was she not the sister-in-law who braided it?
When her lord was alive,
Long enjoying the age of princely rule,
Was she not the sister-in-law accustomed to it?
Her dear, long thick hair,
Gathered atop her head,
Was she not the sister-in-law who bound it?
If hostile enemies came from every side,
While her falcon Manas was alive,
If an unending dispute arose,
Wielding a spear in a warrior’s place,
Breaking their stone fortress,
Was she not the sister-in-law who entered?
The boldest among women,
Was she not your lion of a sister-in-law?
For many six-month spans and many days,
When he persistently left her neglected,
She equaled him in bravery.
Was she not your lion of a sister-in-law?
She did not grieve over this affair,
Your dear sister-in-law Kanykey.
She did not reveal her widowhood,
Nor speak against God.
She never let her spirit be divided.
Kanykey took as her hope
Her sole child, Semetey.
Wandering toward Bukhara, walking on foot,
Your leopard mother Kanykey,
Without a mount, fleeing on foot,
Your noble mother Kanykey
Walked unsparingly, leaning for support.
Almambet’s Syr Barang,
She leaned upon it as a staff.
“If I see Talas safely,
I shall reach the end together with it,” she said.
Regarding it as himself until death,
Alake’s Syr Barang,
Your suffering sister-in-law Kanykey
Said, “I shall keep it as a gift,”
And relentless trouble
Did she not take upon herself?
Almambet’s Syr Barang,
As a staff, from Talas,
Had she not brought it away?
Without shoes, in felt stockings,
The poor soul walked in sorrow.
When the sun sank, shimmering,
She came exhausted and leaned for rest.
Then your mother Kanykey
Leaned upon the great poplar.
That great poplar standing there—
The birds upon its branches,
The creatures fluttered, ready to fly.
The birds in its poplar,
That great poplar standing there—
They stirred, ready to take flight.
When she reached the great poplar,
Its chervil was thick as a wrist.
Its deer, fleeing at a shout of “Go!”
Were like pale cows with white blazes.
Its leaves were like sheets of hide;
As you looked, the blessed place
Had black spiders big as thumbs.
If you looked toward its lower slopes,
Parrots sang and chattered.
They called the tree a plane-tree poplar;
It was a sacred place.
It was the eye of a bubbling spring,
A holy shrine itself.
“With the flesh behind the knees drawn tight,
A place for the emaciated to lie,
For one who has suffered hardship in her village,
For one who has suffered as I have,
A place for the unfortunate to lie.
Ten saints and holy elders—
It is a place of blessing.
For the thin one without food,
For the unfortunate like me,
This great poplar standing here
